title: Lamentations
summary: Lamentations is a biblical book focused on grief over Jerusalem, exile trauma, mercy, and hope.
historical_context: Lamentations gives poetic voice to Jerusalem's devastation while clinging to the Lord's mercy.
ancient_near_east_context: Lamentations belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Lamentations should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Lamentations as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Major Prophets, book 3 of 5, Lamentations contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting grief over Jerusalem, exile trauma, mercy, and hope to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Lamentations as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Lamentations uses poetry, lament within Major Prophets, book 3 of 5 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Lamentations helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional prophetic attribution to the named prophet
Many scholars note later collection and occasional expansion
date_ranges: 8th-6th centuries BCE with later shaping in some books
Final forms often reflect exilic or post-exilic editing
original_audience: Judah and Israel in crisis, facing judgment, exile, and restoration hopes
historical_setting: The late monarchic, exilic, and post-exilic periods
canonical_role: Lamentations anchors grief over Jerusalem, exile trauma, mercy, and hope within Major Prophets, book 3 of 5 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How judgment and hope are balanced

related_objects.notes: Jerusalem is the grieving center of the poems.
The fall of Jerusalem is the historical trauma behind the book.
The poems belong to the crisis of Babylonian exile.
The book gives poetic voice to exile and loss.
Hope appears within grief and covenant appeal.
